processing: Tender leaf is spread to lose about 15% of its moisture, then given kill-green, rolling and two-stage drying, by hand or machine. Hand-made lots use a gentle hot roll and a slow final bake at about 60°C to keep tip, down and colour.
harvest_season: Early spring, from mid-March to around Qingming depending on the account, using one bud with a just-opening leaf.
appearance_dry: Fine, even, tightly curled strips covered in silver down, with a glossy jade-green colour.
appearance_wet: Tender, even and bright green leaf.
taste_profile: Clean, fresh and brisk with a rich, clear fragrance and a light, pure sweetness.

brewing.notes: General guidance for downy bud-grade greens: cooler water, and a slight haze from the down is no fault.

vintage_note: Sold as the current spring harvest and best drunk within about a year. It is a farm-origin tea, so the producer matters as much as the name. A curlier sibling from the same farm is sold under the name Yang'ai Bilüchun.
description:
Yang'ai Maofeng takes its name from the Yang'ai tea farm in the southwestern outskirts of Guiyang, in what is now Huaxi District. Unlike many Chinese teas with a blurry past, this one has a known birthplace and a known start: it is a farm-developed tea from 1960.

The leaf is one bud with a barely opened leaf, spread out to wilt a little before heat is applied. The hand method is careful about the curl: the pan temperature falls from about 140°C to around 100 to 110°C during fixing, and the final bake is slow and low. The aim is to keep the tips, down and green colour whole.

Expect a clear, fragrant cup that is fresh and clean rather than heavy. Downy leaf like this burns easily, so use water that has cooled well below boiling and shorter first steeps.

Look for plenty of silver down and even, tender strips, and ask for the year. If you enjoy it, try another Guizhou maofeng side by side, such as Huangguoshu Maofeng, to see how the same style shifts between farms.
history:
The Yang'ai farm was set up in 1952 and began tea production in 1955, once running to about 10,200 mu of gardens. The maofeng was developed there in 1960. It was named one of Guizhou's four famous local teas in 1984 and a national famous tea by the Ministry of Commerce in 1986.

Exports began after 1975, reaching Hong Kong, Macau, Japan, the United States and others. Until 1997 it was a small planned product at about 3,000 kg a year; reported sales then climbed to nearly 25,000 kg by 2002. In 2003 the farm added a curlier related tea, and the former farm now operates as a company, Guizhou Yang'ai Ecological Tea.
